answers.text: Instruction: always return three lines in this order — delivery date, item and quantity, and any change from the original order. Same order, same three lines, every time.
List every claim by date, amount, category and submitter, then total the amounts at the end. If two lines look like the same claim entered twice, flag it rather than adding both in.
The three-days-out claim doesn't match the 19th being five days after the 14th — that's the error. I'd check the actual call date before this goes out.
62 up from 54 is right for a 15% rise. But 3 late out of 62 isn't a 97% on-time rate, more like 95% — worth flagging before it's sent up.
I'd sign off on Output 2 — it shows the €612,000 and €25,100 behind the 4.1%. Output 1 might well be correct too, but there's no way to check it without re-running the numbers.
Reply 2 — it names the order and credit reference, so it's traceable. Reply 1 doesn't give you anything to check if it came up again.
1. No. 2. Yes. 3. No. 4. No, I'd still hold off with an unvetted tool. 5. No.
I'd redact the pricing terms before pasting any of this into an unvetted tool.
I'd cross-check the report totals against the warehouse system before it goes up to the manager.
Step 1, reading the order email, is the one I'd watch closest.
